one_liner: C library that parses and normalizes street addresses worldwide with a CRF; about 10-65x faster per address than Deepparse's neural parser.
what_it_does: Turns free-form international addresses into labelled components (house_number, road, unit, postcode, city, state, country and about a dozen more) with libpostal_parse_address, and into normalized variants for matching and indexing with libpostal_expand_address ('30 W 26th St' and '30 West Twenty-sixth Street' expand to comparable strings). It also ships a language classifier and near-duplicate hashing helpers. It is a one-address-at-a-time C call after a one-off setup that loads the models; it is not a drop-in for Deepparse, which is a Python library with batching and retraining, and its label set differs. Python, Go, Ruby, Node and other bindings (pypostal and others) wrap the same C API.
how_it_is_fast: Parsing is a linear-chain Conditional Random Field decoded with Viterbi over sparse, hand-engineered features (normalized word, dictionary phrase membership, postal-code and admin context), so each address costs a few sparse dot products per token instead of the embedding lookups and recurrent network passes of a neural tagger; an older greedy averaged-perceptron model format is still loadable. Dictionaries live in double-array tries, weights in compressed sparse matrices and most other data in contiguous arrays, all loaded once at setup. On x86 the build enables SSE2 math routines by default. The README itself says the design optimizes memory first and speed last.
when_to_use: Batch normalization, deduplication or geocoder preprocessing of millions of addresses on CPUs, where a CPU-only throughput of thousands to tens of thousands of addresses per second per process is enough and no GPU is available.
Multilingual, multinational address data (trained on over 1 billion OSM and OpenAddresses records covering every inhabited country) where per-country rule sets are not maintainable.
Building fuzzy address matching on top of a normal search engine or hash table: expand once at index time and once at query time.
Calling from Python, Go, Ruby or Node in-process through an existing binding, instead of standing up a separate model server.
US, UK and Singapore-heavy data, where the optional Senzing model (MODEL=senzing) reports 4.3 percent better parses on Senzing's own test set.
when_not_to_use: Memory- or disk-constrained deployments: the default model is about 1.8 GB (2.2 GB for Senzing) and a parser process sits near 1.9 GB RSS (issue #676 pmap figures); serverless hosts such as AWS Lambda are an open question (issue #538).

Multithreaded in-process parsing: the library keeps one global parser with a single shared context and CRF scratch buffers, 'Make libpostal thread safe' (#34) has been open since 2016 and #102 reports SIGSEGV with 8 threads; scale with processes, which multiplies the memory cost.

Untrusted input without a timeout: a single invalid UTF-8 byte 0xC6 makes parse_address spin at 100 percent CPU in scan_token (#460, open), and invalid characters can drive tokenize_add_tokens into an endless loop and OOM (#548, open).
Windows-first or Apple Silicon builds: Windows needs MSYS2 and MinGW with several open build issues, and ARM builds disable SSE2, which the README says gives poorer performance.
When you need to retrain or fine-tune on your own address style cheaply: Deepparse is built for that, while libpostal's training pipeline works on a 100 GB-plus corpus.

integration.form: shared lib (autotools build of libpostal.so / .a) plus separately downloaded model data
integration.dependencies: autoconf, automake, libtool, pkg-config and curl to build; about 1.8 GB of model data fetched at install (or --disable-data-download); optional CBLAS if cblas.h is found; packages exist in Homebrew and MacPorts
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (AC_PROG_CC_C99); library built at -O2, tools at -O3, scanner always at -O0
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS supported; Windows only via MSYS2/MinGW ('not a priority'); x86 gets -msse2 -DUSE_SSE by default, arm64/aarch64 builds skip SSE2 automatically or need --disable-sse2 on M1
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe: libpostal_parse_address reuses one global address_parser_context and the CRF's single context and Viterbi buffer on every call; serialize calls with a mutex or use one process per core (issues #34, #102).

gotchas: The README's '10-30k addresses / second in a single thread' points to src/bench.c, which times libpostal_expand_address (normalization, not the parser) on one command-line string repeated 100,000 times with clock(); it is not a parse_address throughput figure on varied input. The Deepparse run's 0.00004 s per parse (about 25,000 per second, derived from page data) is the only independent parser number.

Harness flaws in the cited Deepparse comparison: libpostal was timed through pypostal in a Python loop inside memory_profiler's @profile, whose line tracing takes a memory sample on each executed line, so the libpostal figure is pessimistic; Deepparse's committed speed_test_evaluation.py calls process_fn() without its required batch_size argument (a TypeError as written) and reopens its result file in 'w' mode on every batch size; the 'batch of more than 1' column is a mean over batch sizes 2-512, and the GPU fastText-light row shows that mean (0.0037 s) slower than batch 1 (0.0028 s).

Before 1.1.4 (fix of 2025-10-18, #676) context->separators was never cleared between parses, so RSS grew about 20-30 MB per 500,000 parses; the array is not read by the parser's feature function in the current source, so parse results were not affected, but long-running services on older builds (including whatever version the 2023 benchmark used) leak.

Issue #597 reported out-of-bounds writes in the SSE path (remez9_0_log2_sse assumes buffers are multiples of 4 doubles and realloc ignores alignment); it is closed (2024) but the issue page does not show the fix, so test SSE builds under a sanitizer if you vendor an older release.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued siblings parse addresses: use libpostal to parse and expand addresses before indexing them in Tantivy, Manticore or PISA, and pick it over RapidFuzz when matching must understand address abbreviations, transliteration and component structure rather than raw string similarity.
verified_claims_summary: Deepparse's authors (a competing project) timed about 183,000 multinational addresses on Linux with Python 3.11, Torch 2.0 and CUDA 11.7 on 2023-03-21 (an RTX 2080 GPU per their paper's search snippets; CPU model, libpostal version and build flags not stated): libpostal via pypostal took about 0.00004 s per address, against Deepparse fastText at about 0.0004 s on GPU and 0.0026 s on CPU when batched (about 10x and 65x, derived from page data) and 0.0023 s and 0.0128 s at batch size 1. The libpostal row is a single unbatched number reused in both tables, so the comparison mixes a CRF in a Python loop with neural models at varying batch sizes.
status_note: Maintained at a slow cadence by the original author (releases 1.1.0 to 1.1.4 in September-October 2025, Senzing data v1.2.0 merged 2025-12-06, many 2019-2023 bug reports still open); MIT-licensed code, copyable, but it needs the separately downloaded ~1.8 GB model, is not thread-safe, and the cited speed comparison comes from a competitor's harness with the flaws listed under gotchas (pessimistic for libpostal, broken script for Deepparse).
